abstract: No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $Θ_0, Θ_1, Θ_2, \dots$ with $Θ_k \circ Θ_j = Θ_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $Θ_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two. Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.
title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)

abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.
title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits

abstract: For which sets F of edge modifications do a graph G and the modified graph share a maximum cardinality search (MCS) ordering? We prove that they do whenever, along every proper common MCS prefix, each unchosen vertex's neighbour count in the second graph exceeds its count in the first by zero or one. In particular, inserting or deleting any matching, or flipping a single edge, preserves a common ordering, and under the same hypothesis every common MCS prefix extends to a full common ordering without backtracking. Neither part of the hypothesis can simply be dropped: inserting a triangle, a P_4 or a 2P_3 shows that the +1 bound cannot be relaxed to +2, and a disjoint mixed insert/delete pair shows that the one-directional condition is needed. For the canonical ordering (smallest-index tie-breaking) under a single-edge update, an insertion can first change the ordering only strictly between the endpoints' positions, and a deletion only at the later endpoint; when no break fires, the ordering is unchanged. A boolean-adjacency executable refines the abstract probe-then-repair update. All of these results, including the four obstructions, are proved in Lean 4 over Mathlib, re-checked by independent kernel checkers, and registered in the Palomar registry. On paper we further show that the first break of an insertion is located in O((deg(v)+1) log n) time, independent of the window length. We claim no worst-case asymptotic speedup over recomputation.
title: How rigid is maximum cardinality search? Stability and locality of MCS orderings under edge updates, verified in Lean

abstract: We study networks with an unbounded number of processes sharing some natural counters that can be decremented, incremented and tested to zero. We look at two safety problems: the first one asks whether there is a network with an execution bringing a process in a given final state and the other one asks the execution to bring all the processes in the final state. In their full generality, these two problems are undecidable, but we show that decidability can be regained by either using a single counter or by forbidding the use of zero-tests (as it is is the case in Vector Addition Systems with States). For these decidable cases, we obtain low complexity results, the problems being solvable either in non-deterministic logarithmic space or in polynomial time.
title: Safety Analysis of Parameterized Networks with Shared Counters

abstract: The QBF Gallery 2026 is the latest evaluation event of (dependency) quantified Boolean formula (QBF) solving technology. Its goal is to assess the current state-of-the-art, enable the evaluation of novel solvers on newly curated benchmark instances and present the progress made since the previous competition. This report discusses the solvers, instances and tools submitted by the community and introduces new benchmark collections for evaluation. We evaluate solvers in three tracks, reflecting most common input formats in (dependency) QBF solving. In addition to those main evaluations, we investigate effects of preprocessing and include a track of new crafted benchmark families. The results are analyzed using various metrics and complementary statistics on solver similarities, different memory limitations and performance across formula families. Finally, the dedicated benchmarks for each track are made available as an artifact to support future research and reproducible evaluation.
title: The QBF Gallery 2026

abstract: A program logic proved sound against one effectful semantics need not remain sound when the effect is re-implemented, yet the semantic relationship between reasoning before and after a change of effect is usually left implicit and re-established by hand. This paper provides a uniform, proof-relevant account of it. Working in realizability, where a notion of computation determines a model whose entailments carry explicit program evidence, we introduce simulations between effectful realizability cores, generalizing Longley's applicative morphisms to computation over an arbitrary strong monad. A single simulation transports the source logic along a ladder: it induces a morphism of the associated evidenced frames and, functorially, of the induced triposes. These passages are $2$-fully-faithful, so the three levels agree and a change of effect carries the entire higher-order program logic together with the evidence witnessing each derivation. A computationally dense simulation moreover computes a modality on the source logic, a nucleus through which the transport factors and which marks exactly the reasoning stable under the change, read off from the translation rather than postulated. This recovers known examples such as the double-negation modality of classical realizability, and examples such as sheafification arise from a modal refinement of the construction. Overall, the framework makes a change of effect a first-class object, one that can be composed, factored through its modality, and shown in cases not to exist, opening a path to transporting verified reasoning across effects.
title: Evidence-Carrying Transport Across Effects

abstract: Quantum loops may execute arbitrarily many iterations, and understanding their runtime behavior requires knowing how often they terminate, how long terminating runs take, and how common very long runs are. We develop a compositional weakest-precondition framework for analyzing these properties on possibly infinite-dimensional state spaces. It uses parameterized predicates: families of quantum effects indexed by a positive observation scale. These families retain runtime information even when the expected runtime is infinite and can be reused through sequential composition and nested loops. We prove that weakest-precondition equations for loops have unique solutions in the parameterized predicate domain. From the asymptotic behavior of the derived weakest preconditions, we then recover these runtime properties and quantify the influence of very long terminating executions. For the classic discrete-time quantum walk on the one-dimensional infinite line with one absorbing boundary at the origin and the Hadamard gate as its coin operator, we verify its termination probability $2/π$, conditional mean $π/2$, and logarithmic growth of the conditional capped second moment. We then reuse the walk's specification to verify the termination probability and conditional mean runtime of an outer loop that repeatedly invokes it.
title: Parameterized Weakest-Precondition Calculus for Fine-grained Properties of Quantum Loops

abstract: Although modern SAT solvers have made remarkable progress, they still exploit formula structure only to a limited extent. We present two techniques that make SAT solving more structure-aware and provide experimental results showing their promise. The first technique ``$\mathit{melts}$'' the formula by reducing interaction between its parts. This is achieved by adding new variables, using existential quantifiers, and applying a procedure called partial quantifier elimination. The second technique exploits the notion of a $\mathit{local}$ $\mathit{proof}$. The latter establishes that a formula is unsatisfiable by proving that certain literals of its clauses are redundant. We show that using local proofs makes SAT solving more formula-specific.
title: On Structure-Aware SAT Solving

Denote $(A_n(u))$ the linear recursive sequence having characteristic polynomial $P_u(X)$ and initial terms $A_0,\ldots,A_{q+1}\in \mathbb{Z}$ such that at least one of them is non-zero. title: Common values of linear recurrences related to Ankeny-Brauer-Chowla polynomials

abstract: Let $K/\mathbf Q_p$ be unramified, with $p>2$. For a $1$-motive with constant lattice, split torus, and good abelian quotient, we compute the semistable extension complex from toric valuations and formal-group logarithms. A canonical monodromy boundary exists for every semistable representation; it detects splitting over crystalline periods and the increase in monodromy rank. For the stated $1$-motives, this boundary and the unramified quotient recover the restricted local Tate pairing, with exponential radicals. Nonsplit elliptic examples, Raynaud uniformization, and a height-one positive-period bound explain the geometric range. For toric motives we construct actual periods, convergent Robba bases, and integral action matrices. A toric basis family has perfect projective/trace-zero matrix duality, including its exact integral defect. An explicit residue-zero solution operator constructs every dual Herr class. Applied componentwise, the same operator gives relative full dual lifts for general constant-lattice $1$-motives once their coefficient sequence is specified. Finally, finite-base coefficient traces realize division-tower Iwasawa cohomology for any Tate lattice, and the period cup pairing equals the arithmetic group-ring pairing.
title: Semistable 1-Motives: Monodromy, Explicit Periods, and Local Duality

abstract: We prove that the $n$-th element of the Ulam sequence, a somewhat mysterious recursively-defined sequence of positive integers, has size $e^{O(\sqrt{n})}$; previous upper bounds were exponential in $n$. Our argument uses an additive-combinatorial lemma, possibly of independent interest, about covering finite difference sets with multiplicatively short intervals. The proofs are due to ChatGPT.
title: The Ulam sequence grows subexponentially

abstract: Let $q=2^m$ for an even $m\geq 6$ and let $d=s(q-1)+1$ with $4s\equiv5\pmod{q+1}$. In this paper, the correlation distribution between a binary m-sequence of period $q^2-1$ and its $d$-decimation is considered. The cross-correlation function takes seven values $q(i-1)-1$ for $0\leq i\leq 6$, and we determine their frequencies based on the study of low-degree self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and three mixed Kloosterman sums, which are finally expressed in terms of $K_m(1)$ and $K_m(ω)$, where $K_m(\cdot)$ is the Kloomsterman sum on the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $ω$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_4$.
title: Correlation distribution for a class of Niho exponents via self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and Kloosterman sums

abstract: The Frobenius angles of non-CM elliptic curves and the Hecke angles of non-CM newforms are equidistributed with respect to the Sato--Tate measure, while for Kloosterman angles, this is known on average over natural families. We study the fluctuations around these laws in large families, for smooth test functions. We prove an unconditional central limit theorem for Frobenius angles of elliptic curves for a much larger class of test functions than previously considered; earlier results assumed the Riemann hypothesis for $L$-functions of Hecke eigenforms of full level. This result follows from a general framework, developed here, which yields Gaussian moments for statistics of sequences in $[0,1]$ varying over families. In this framework, independence is replaced by two quantitative conditions: approximate independence at distinct indices, and convergence of the family averages to the Weyl limits at a suitable rate. As further applications, we extend central limit theorems for Kloosterman angles and for Hecke angles of newforms to larger classes of test functions, the latter with the weight and the level varying simultaneously. We also treat the dilated angles $αθ$ for integers $α\geq2$, whose limiting distribution is uniform. Finally, we discuss sharp statistics, obtaining a central limit theorem for Hecke angles and explaining the obstruction for the other two families.
title: Central limit theorems for Frobenius, Hecke and Kloosterman angles

abstract: We construct a smooth projective Calabi--Yau threefold $X_5$ over $\mathbb F_5$ with $b_3(X_5)=0$ and $b_2(X_5)=31$. Consequently, $X_5$ has no smooth proper lifting to characteristic zero, including over ramified bases. To our knowledge, this is the first smooth projective Calabi--Yau threefold with this property in characteristic $p>3$. The threefold is a crepant resolution of the Kummer quotient of the self-fiber product of a rational elliptic surface. We prove the vanishing of its third Betti number by semistable reduction and point counts. A birational double-octic model gives a direct obstruction to lifting to the ring of Witt vectors of length two, through an explicit inconsistent system of linear equations for the branch data. We also determine the Hodge and crystalline cohomology: the threefold is infinitesimally rigid, its crystalline cohomology is torsion-free, and its third de Rham cohomology vanishes. Its Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence has exactly two nonzero differentials, both of rank one on the second page.
title: A projective Calabi--Yau threefold in characteristic 5 non-liftable to characteristic 0

abstract: We prove uniform tightness of Hecke neighbours of any probability measure of positive entropy that is invariant and ergodic under the diagonal flow. As an application, we confirm a conjecture of Einsiedler concerning a homogeneous dynamics analogue of an equidistribution theorem of Johnson and Rudolph on the torus. We also obtain applications to continued-fraction patterns in arithmetic sequences and to the \(p\)-adic Littlewood conjecture. Our proof studies escape of mass using dynamics on the boundary of the Chabauty compactification of the space of lattices, together with averaging operators defined by leafwise measures along horospherical subgroups.
title: Equidistribution of Hecke neighbours and continued fraction patterns

abstract: We show that for every integer $n\ge2$ that is not a power of two there are constants $c_n>0$ and $B_n>2$ such that $s(C_n^r)\ge c_nB_n^r$ for all $r\ge1$. For powers of two, Harborth's formula gives growth rate exactly $2$. For the remaining even exponents, the previous lower bounds were of order $r2^r$. When $n=2m$ with $m\ge3$ odd, we prove the transfer inequality \[ A_n(H\oplus C_n^5)\ \ge\ 12\,A_n(H\oplus C_n)+8\,A_n(H\oplus C_m), \] where $A_n(G)$ is the maximal length of a sequence over $G$ without an $n$-term zero-sum subsequence and $H$ is any finite abelian group whose exponent divides $n$. The transfer extends a configuration of Elsholtz to twenty full cyclic fibers. Combined with a nine-point binary construction for $2m$-term zero-sums over $C_m^r$, it gives bases at least $2.0341$ that tend to $2.0394\ldots$; combined with a finite-field construction, it gives $s(C_6^r)\ge c\cdot 2.0491^r$. For exponents divisible by $4$ that are not powers of two, we obtain a base above two from a weighted random construction on the eighteen-point configuration of Wang and Zeng.
title: Cyclic fibers and exponential lower bounds for Erdős--Ginzburg--Ziv constants

abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.
title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.
title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration

abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.
title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems

abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.
title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics

abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.
title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models

abstract: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).
title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs

abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.
title: CARGO: Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Preventive Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving
